traveler: Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd ibn Muhammad al-Baghdadi (Junayd of Baghdad)
title: The Glass and the Silk: the Sober Master of Baghdad, his Shop, and the Disciple he Turned Away
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Baghdad, the glass-seller's son
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources give only c. 215 AH, with the birth placed as early as 210 AH, and no day or month anywhere
stops.campa: A son is born in Baghdad to a family of Persian stock and named Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd ibn Muhammad. The father deals in glassware, which fastens on the household the byname al-Qawariri, the glass-seller. The boy will carry two trades in his own name before he carries a doctrine: al-Qawariri from his father, al-Khazzaz from the silk he will sell himself. The quarter of the city is not recorded. A modern attribution to Karkh rests on an encyclopedia entry that would not open, and its coordinate does not match Karkh.
suggested_refs: The Abbasid capital on both banks of the Tigris in the reign of al-Ma'mun

stops.name: Nihawand, the town inside the name
stops.date_confidence: genealogical only; the nisba is undated and no source places Junayd in the town
stops.campa: Six hundred miles east of the Tigris stands Nihawand, in the Zagros country of western Persia, from which the family traces its descent and from which Junayd inherits the nisba al-Nahawandi. He does not go there. No source places him in the town, and none puts him in correspondence with anyone living there. The name travels west with his grandfathers and stays in his title long after the journey that earned it is forgotten. Persia will reach him instead through Baghdad, in books and in visitors.
suggested_refs: Nihawand in the Zagros, ancestral seat of the Nahawandi line

stops.name: Baghdad, the orphan and his uncle
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source dates the father's death or the boy's entry into his uncle's house
stops.campa: The father dies while the boy is small, and Junayd is taken into the house of his mother's brother, Sari al-Saqati, a dealer in scrap turned ascetic, who becomes his master. Sari sets the order of the training and prays that his nephew be given hadith before tasawwuf, and not tasawwuf before hadith. The whole shape of the later school sits in that prayer: the law first, the states after. The year of the father's death is not recorded, and the boy's age at it is given nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The house of Sari al-Saqati in Baghdad, first school of the Junaydiya

stops.name: Mecca, the boy defines thankfulness
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the age of seven is Attar's, and no year is given in any source
stops.campa: Sari takes the child on the pilgrimage to the House toward which Muhammad turned the prayer, and in the Mosque of the Sanctuary four hundred shaykhs are disputing the meaning of shukr, thankfulness. The uncle prompts the seven-year-old to speak. He answers, and the four hundred agree that no better definition can be made. Arberry's translation of Attar sets the scene at Mecca; the standard encyclopedia article sets the same episode in the Prophet's Mosque at Medina. The two are not reconciled anywhere consulted.
stops.quote: Thankfulness means that you should not disobey God by means of the favour which He has bestowed on you, nor make of His favour a source of disobedience.
stops.quote_source: Attar of Nishapur, Muslim Saints and Mystics: Episodes from the Tadhkirat al-Auliya, trans. A.J. Arberry, chapter 'Abo 'l-Qasem al-Jonaid', p. 269
suggested_refs: The Masjid al-Haram at Mecca, one of the two mosques claimed for the shukr episode

stops.name: Medina, the mosque the other version names
stops.date_confidence: contested; the venue is disputed between sources and no year is given for it
stops.campa: Four days north of Mecca stands the mosque built around the Prophet's own house, where Muhammad lies buried and where the second version of the story puts the four hundred shaykhs and the boy who silences them. The stop is here because the contradiction is real and neither side of it is weak: one fetched primary translation says the Sanctuary at Mecca, one standard article says al-Masjid an-Nabawi. Whichever mosque held them, the sentence that survives is the same, and it is the earliest the tradition puts in his mouth.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi at Medina, the rival setting for the shukr episode

stops.name: Baghdad, the teachers who could not have taught him
stops.date_confidence: the death dates are attested; the pupillage they are supposed to prove is not
stops.campa: The lists of his masters carry names the calendar refuses. Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam dies at Mecca in 224 of the Hijra, when Junayd is about eight and has never left Baghdad. Bishr al-Hafi dies three years after that, and the record of Bishr's own transmitters does not include him. Both names sit in the standard rosters all the same. What the rosters preserve is not attendance but lineage, a chain of authority assembled backward by men who needed the jurist of Baghdad to descend from somebody.
suggested_refs: The isnad lists of al-Junayd's teachers in the Arabic biographical dictionaries
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam'

stops.name: Baghdad, hadith first and the states after
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the teacher list is attested, the sequence and the dating are not
stops.campa: The teachers who can be placed in the same room with him are Sari al-Saqati, al-Harith al-Muhasibi, al-Hasan ibn Arafa, and Abu Thawr al-Kalbi. He learns hadith, then jurisprudence, then the discipline of the states, in that order and by his uncle's design. Baghdad in these years is the largest school in the world and the sciences are not yet walled off from one another. A man can carry a law book into a session on the accounting of the soul and nobody in the room thinks him lost.
suggested_refs: The teaching circles of ninth-century Baghdad, where law and mysticism shared students

stops.name: Baghdad, the fatwa at twenty
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the age of twenty is the figure the Arabic sources give, without a year
stops.campa: In the study circle of Ibrahim ibn Khalid, called Abu Thawr, Junayd is permitted to issue formal legal opinions at about the age of twenty, with his teacher sitting there while he gives them. The Arabic tradition remembers him afterward as the man who combined the heart of the ascetic with the intellect of the jurist. Later writers file him as Shafi'i. Abu Thawr's circle is not the school of Sufyan al-Thawri, and the habit of calling it Thawri confuses two jurists a century apart.
suggested_refs: The circle of Abu Thawr al-Kalbi in Baghdad, where al-Junayd was licensed to give fatwas

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Muhasibi dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; 243 AH
stops.campa: Al-Harith al-Muhasibi, who taught the scrutiny of one's own motives until the practice took his name, dies in Baghdad in 243 of the Hijra. From him Junayd takes the habit of turning the instrument inward before turning it on anybody else, which is why the school he will lead never produces an ecstatic who cannot say what state he is in. The teacher dies out of favour with the traditionists of the city. The pupil will spend fifty years avoiding that particular death.
suggested_refs: The doctrine of muhasaba, self-examination, as al-Muhasibi taught it in Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, silk and glass
stops.date_confidence: the trade is attested; the duration is not, and no source consulted supplies one
stops.campa: He keeps a shop and takes no payment for teaching. The Arabic tradition gives glassware to the father and silk to the son, which is where the two bynames come from; the English hagiography has Junayd himself selling glasses. Both cannot be right and neither is discarded here. What the sources agree on is narrower: he lives by the trade and spends the rest of his hours in prayer. How long he goes on as a merchant who prays rather than a master who teaches is a figure nobody supplies, and the forty years in circulation rest on nothing.
suggested_refs: The silk and glass markets of ninth-century Baghdad, livelihood of the sober school's founder

stops.name: Baghdad, the dream that gives permission
stops.date_confidence: traditional; hagiographic and undated
stops.campa: Sari presses his nephew to speak in public. Junayd refuses, on the ground that a man does not appoint himself, and holds out until he sees the Prophet in a dream and takes what he sees as leave to begin. The refusal is doctrine before it is biography. The sober school starts from the position that authority arrives from outside the self and cannot be assumed by anyone who wants it. Nicholson relays the episode from the Persian hagiographers, who are the only source there is for it.
stops.quote: Sari al-Saqati frequently urged Junayd to speak in public, but Junayd was unwilling to consent until he received guidance from the Prophet in a dream.
stops.quote_source: Reynold A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (London, 1914), Project Gutenberg ebook #67388
suggested_refs: Nicholson's Mystics of Islam, relaying the Persian hagiographers on Junayd's licence to preach

stops.name: Baghdad, eighteen died and twenty-two fainted
stops.date_confidence: legend; undated and uncorroborated outside hagiography
stops.campa: Of the first forty who come to hear him, tradition holds that eighteen die where they sit and twenty-two fall unconscious. The number reappears across the corpus of Sufi legend, attached to other masters in other rooms, and nothing outside hagiography records it. It is kept here for what it says about the reputation being built. The sober master of Baghdad, the one who spends his life warning against ecstatic speech, is remembered as having killed half a room with a sermon.
suggested_refs: The legend of the first forty listeners, in Attar and the later biographical tradition

stops.name: Baghdad, unity taught as a syllabus
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the claim of priority belongs to the Arabic biographical tradition itself
stops.campa: He is credited with being the first to set out the doctrines of divine unity as formal instruction inside a Sufi circle, rather than as private counsel given to one man at a time, and the Baghdad school forms around that teaching. His disciples call him sayyid al-ta'ifa, master of the community. The claim of firstness comes from the tradition that has an interest in it and cannot be tested against rooms nobody wrote down. What can be observed is that after him the teaching has a syllabus.
suggested_refs: The Baghdad school of sober Sufism, the Junaydiya, as later writers name it

stops.name: Baghdad, what Sufism is
stops.date_confidence: undated saying; placed here within the teaching years
stops.campa: Asked what tasawwuf is, he answers with a list rather than a definition, and the list is all discipline: purification, separation, suppression, refusal, attachment, counsel, fidelity, and the Law. Kalabadhi records it among a chain of answers given by different masters to the same question. A sentence often welded onto the front of it, about dying to oneself and being resurrected in God, is not in Kalabadhi at all; Nicholson prints something like it with no name attached. The two are kept apart here.
stops.quote: It is the purification of the heart from associating with created beings, separation from natural characteristics, suppression of human qualities, avoiding the temptations of the carnal soul, taking up the qualities of the spirit, attachment to the sciences of reality, using what is more proper to the eternal, counselling all the community, being truly faithful to God, and following the Prophet according to the Law.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr al-Kalabadhi, The Doctrine of the Sufis (Kitab al-Ta'arruf), trans. A.J. Arberry (Cambridge, 1935), ch. I, p. 10
suggested_refs: Kalabadhi's chapter of definitions, where each master answers the same question in turn
sources: Kalabadhi, The Doctrine of the Sufis, trans. Arberry, p. 10

stops.name: Baghdad, the colour of the vessel
stops.date_confidence: undated saying; placed here within the teaching years
stops.campa: Asked about the gnostic, the one who knows, he gives a line that will be quoted for a thousand years and misquoted for most of them. Arberry's Kalabadhi has water and a vessel and a question about the knower. The popular English has a cup, a colour taken on, and a question about divine self-disclosure, which is a different claim in a prettier sentence. The Arabic makes the smaller and harder one: the knowing man has no colour of his own, and shows the shape of whatever hour he is in.
stops.quote: The colour of the water is the colour of the vessel.
stops.quote_source: Abu Bakr al-Kalabadhi, The Doctrine of the Sufis, trans. A.J. Arberry, p. 139
suggested_refs: Kalabadhi's chapter on gnosis, p. 139, where Arberry glosses the gnostic as the son of his time
sources: Kalabadhi, The Doctrine of the Sufis, trans. Arberry, p. 139
Michael A. Sells, Early Islamic Mysticism (1996), cited but not reachable

stops.name: Baghdad, the empty heart
stops.date_confidence: undated saying; recorded two centuries later by Hujwiri
stops.campa: He is asked what poverty is and gives a definition with no destitution in it. Faqr is a condition of the heart and not of the purse, and the phenomena that must leave it are everything created. Hujwiri sets the saying down in his chapter on poverty two centuries later, in Persian, from a chain of Baghdad transmitters, and Nicholson turns it into English eight hundred years after that. Three languages and a millennium of copying have not managed to add a word to the sentence.
stops.quote: When his heart is empty of phenomena he is poor.
stops.quote_source: Ali ibn Uthman al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. R.A. Nicholson (Gibb Memorial Series, 1911), ch. II, p. 27
suggested_refs: Hujwiri's Kashf al-Mahjub, chapter on poverty, the earliest Persian handbook of Sufism
sources: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. Nicholson, ch. II, p. 27

stops.name: Baghdad, the address to the poor
stops.date_confidence: undated saying; recorded two centuries later by Hujwiri
stops.campa: He speaks to the fuqara, the voluntary poor of his own circle, and aims the warning at the danger nearest to them: that poverty accepted for God becomes a rank, and rank acquires an audience, and the audience follows a man into the room where he is supposed to be alone with God. In the same chapter Hujwiri preserves his answer to Ibn Ata on whether wealth or poverty stands better before the judgment, which does not settle the question so much as move it somewhere colder.
stops.quote: O ye that are poor, ye are known through God, and are honoured for the sake of God: take heed how ye behave when ye are alone with Him.
stops.quote_source: al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. R.A. Nicholson, ch. II, p. 27
suggested_refs: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, ch. II, pp. 23 and 27, on poverty and on the exchange with Ibn Ata
sources: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. Nicholson, ch. II, pp. 23 and 27

stops.name: Baghdad, the second unity, and thirty-one letters
stops.date_confidence: the writings are attested; none of them is individually dated
stops.campa: He writes. Some thirty-one short treatises and letters survive under his name, on unity, on annihilation and subsistence, on how a seeker should conduct himself, and in them he divides esoteric tawhid into two kinds. In the first, the man declaring God's oneness still keeps his own individuality. In the second and higher, he does not. Abdel-Kader's edition of 1962 prints the Arabic and the English together; the paraphrase in wide circulation, drowned in seas and self-effaced, is not his translation.
stops.quote: The second type of esoteric Tawhid consists in existence without individuality (shakhs) before God with no third person as intermediary between them, a figure over which His decrees pass as He in His Omnipotence determines, and that he should be sunk in the flooding seas of His Unity, completely obliterated both from himself and from God's call to him and his answer to God.
stops.quote_source: Ali Hassan Abdel-Kader, The Life, Personality and Writings of al-Junayd (Luzac, 1962), p. 177
suggested_refs: The Rasa'il of al-Junayd, thirty-one surviving treatises and letters
sources: Abdel-Kader, The Life, Personality and Writings of al-Junayd (1962), pp. 75 and 177

stops.name: Baghdad, the Egyptian's sayings arrive without the Egyptian
stops.date_confidence: the transmission is undated; Dhu'l-Nun's death is placed c. 859-862
stops.campa: Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri dies at Giza and is buried in the City of the Dead, and his sayings reach Baghdad. Whether they reach Junayd from the man or from a page is exactly what the sources refuse to say. Some reports have a meeting, others only transmission at second hand, and the disagreement is left standing. No source places Junayd in Egypt at any point in his life. Dhu'l-Nun's one documented journey to Baghdad was made under guard, on a charge of heresy, the year before Junayd was born.
suggested_refs: The sayings of Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri as they entered the Baghdad circles
sources: Sufi biographical tradition, contested and unresolved

stops.name: Nishapur, letters into Khurasan
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the correspondence is undated and was not independently verified in this pass
stops.campa: His correspondence runs east into Khurasan, to Abu Uthman al-Hiri of Nishapur, and the Baghdad doctrine of sobriety travels with it. Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi, often named among his correspondents and just as often placed at Rayy, had in fact left Rayy for Balkh and then for Nishapur, where he died in 871. Whatever passed between them belongs to Khurasan and not to the plateau town the reference books give. Junayd himself never goes east. The letters go for him.
suggested_refs: The Khurasani correspondence network linking Baghdad, Nishapur, Balkh and Bestam
sources: Sufi biographical tradition on Junayd's correspondents

stops.name: Baghdad, the Persian turned into Arabic
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the atlas entry for Abu Yazid al-Bistami places the translation c. 900, and no source fixes a year
stops.campa: The sayings of Abu Yazid al-Bistami, spoken in Persian in a small town under the Alburz, are put into Arabic in Baghdad by a man who never met him; the Iranica entry states flatly that no record of any meeting exists. Sari al-Saqati, uncle to one and familiar to the other's circle, is the hinge. The translation makes the drunken master legible to the capital, and hands Hujwiri the terms of a quarrel that outlasts both men: the Tayfuriya against the Junaydiya, intoxication against sobriety, set at odds by a book neither of them wrote.
suggested_refs: Hujwiri's division of the schools into Tayfuriya and Junaydiya
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami' (relayed; the site returned HTTP 403)

stops.name: Baghdad, the first door of Junayd
stops.date_confidence: the atlas entry for al-Hallaj gives June 876; the encyclopedic sources give no year at all
stops.campa: A young man of eighteen out of Fars, already clothed in the Sufi habit by Amr al-Makki at Basra, presents himself at the door in Baghdad. Junayd tests him and sends him south again rather than keep him, citing the state of the country: the Zanj rebels hold the marshland below Basra in black, and the capital is not settled. The refusal will be read afterward as prophecy. At the time it is a master declining a candidate, a thing masters do weekly, which nobody records unless the candidate turns out to be al-Hallaj.
suggested_refs: The Zanj rebellion in the marshes below Basra, 869-883

stops.name: Baghdad, the advice against the pilgrimage
stops.date_confidence: attested; the departure is placed at the crushing of the Zanj rebellion, c. 883
stops.campa: The Zanj rebellion is crushed and the roads open again. Al-Hallaj, worn down by the quarrel between his father-in-law and Amr al-Makki, announces that he is going to Mecca. Junayd advises against it. Al-Hallaj goes anyway, and comes back a preacher with a following and no master's permission, known in the city through two channels at once: the frontier volunteers who heard him at Ahwaz, and Junayd's own circle, who listen to what he is saying and do not care for it.
suggested_refs: The pilgrim road from Baghdad to Mecca, taken against the advice of Junayd

stops.name: Baghdad, the midnight door
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated, and the setting is disputed between sources
stops.campa: He comes back to the same door at midnight and answers the question of who is there with the sentence that will kill him, ana al-Haqq, I am the Truth. Junayd refuses him admission and tells him what wood he will one day stain. Whether the words were first said at this door or first shouted in a mosque is a thing the sources do not agree on, and the versions are not reconciled here: one is a private scene between master and disciple, the other a public act with witnesses and a charge attached.
suggested_refs: The two rival settings of the utterance ana al-Haqq, private consultation and public mosque

stops.name: Baghdad, Amr al-Makki's judgment
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated
stops.campa: Amr ibn Uthman al-Makki, who gave al-Hallaj the Sufi habit at Basra and belongs to the same Baghdad milieu, says he would have killed the man with his own hands over what he has been saying. Junayd's withdrawal is quieter and colder. He stops answering, and the school stops counting al-Hallaj among its own. The distance between those two responses is the distance between a quarrel and a doctrine, and only one of the two can be built on for three hundred years.
suggested_refs: Amr ibn Uthman al-Makki, of the Baghdad circle, on al-Hallaj

stops.name: Baghdad, the gibbet foretold
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated and attested nowhere outside the Massignon-derived tradition
stops.campa: The break is complete. Tradition, following Massignon's reconstruction, has Junayd naming the wood years before the sentence, and that prediction is the hinge the whole later legend turns on: the sober master who saw it coming, the drunk disciple who walked into it regardless. The disownment is attested nowhere outside that tradition, and it is not treated here as more than tradition. What is attested is that after this al-Hallaj has no teacher in Baghdad willing to stand behind him.
suggested_refs: Louis Massignon, La Passion de al-Hallaj, source of the disownment tradition

stops.name: Baghdad, Ghulam Khalil brings the Sufis to court
stops.date_confidence: traditional; modern scholarship dates the campaign c. 264-266 AH
stops.campa: The traditionist Ghulam Khalil moves against the Sufis of the capital, and several of Junayd's associates are brought before the qadi on charges of heresy. Junayd is not among them. The licence to give legal opinions, earned in Abu Thawr's circle thirty years earlier, is the reason usually given, and it is the argument of his whole life reduced to one administrative fact: a mystic who is also a jurist is harder to prosecute. The encyclopedia page on Ghulam Khalil would not open during this research.
suggested_refs: The Ghulam Khalil inquisition against the Baghdad Sufis, c. 264-266 AH
sources: al-Sulami, Tabaqat al-Sufiyya tradition as summarized in Karamustafa, Sufism: The Formative Period

stops.name: Baghdad, Shibli sent to the salt market
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode is hagiographic and undated
stops.campa: Abu Bakr al-Shibli, a chamberlain who has held office in this city, comes asking for the jewel of divine knowledge. Junayd tells him it is not for sale at a price he can pay and would be got too cheap as a gift, then sends him to trade salt in the market and to beg in the streets where he was once known, for years, before accepting him. Ahmad al-Jariri is counted beside him among the leading students, and it is al-Jariri who carries the teaching forward when the master is gone.
stops.quote: I cannot sell it, for you have not the price thereof; and if I give it you, you will have gained it cheaply.
stops.quote_source: Reynold A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (London, 1914), Project Gutenberg ebook #67388
suggested_refs: Attar's account of Shibli's novitiate under al-Junayd, relayed by Nicholson

stops.name: Baghdad, the men of the same milieu
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the associations are undated and were not independently verified in this pass
stops.campa: Ruwaym ibn Ahmad teaches in the city in the same years, and Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz argues with the circle over fana and baqa, the passing away of the self and its subsistence afterward. Later compilers sometimes write Ruwaym into Junayd's initiatic chain; the chains themselves run through Sari al-Saqati and not through him. The Baghdad of these decades holds more sober masters than the lineages have room to name, and the lineages solve that problem by naming fewer.
suggested_refs: The second generation of Baghdad Sufis: Ruwaym ibn Ahmad, Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz, Ahmad al-Jariri
sources: Sufi biographical tradition, not independently verified

stops.name: Baghdad, the last wird
stops.date_confidence: traditional; hagiographic, and no day or month is recorded
stops.campa: He is old and dying, and he goes on praying. Asked why, he answers that this is his wird, the portion a man owes daily, and that it does not stop because the body has. The scene comes from the Arabic hagiographic tradition and is the kind of thing that gets attributed to every master in the end. It is kept because it is consistent with everything else recorded of him: no last vision, no ecstatic utterance, no summing up, only the practice, finished on time.
suggested_refs: The wird, the daily portion of recitation, in the discipline of the Baghdad school

stops.name: Baghdad, the death of the master of the community
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year within a range of 296-298 AH; no day, no month, and no place of death beyond the city
stops.campa: Junayd dies in Baghdad at seventy-nine or eighty. The Arabic sources give 297 or 298 of the Hijra, the English gives 910, and the full range runs from 296; nothing consulted narrows it, and no source names a place of death beyond the city itself. He has outlived the uncle who raised him by forty-three years, taught for most of fifty, and leaves behind a school with a vocabulary, a syllabus, and a standing rule against saying more than a man knows.
suggested_refs: The disputed death year: 296, 297 or 298 AH, 910 CE in the Western reckoning

stops.name: Baghdad, the prayer said seven times
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the number of repetitions is uncorroborated
stops.campa: The funeral prayer is said over him seven times, tradition holds, because the mourners keep arriving faster than the body can be carried the short distance to the ground. The number is not corroborated anywhere, and it is the kind of detail that grows in the telling from one repetition to seven. What the story is built to carry is the crowd rather than the count. A man who spent decades behind a shop shutter, taking no fee for what he taught, is given by his own tradition a funeral the rite cannot get through in a single attempt.
suggested_refs: The funeral of al-Junayd in Karkh, as the hagiographers describe it
sources: Sufi hagiographic tradition, widely repeated and uncorroborated

stops.name: Baghdad, laid beside Sari al-Saqati
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is buried in the Shunuziyya, the old cemetery on the west bank in Karkh that grew around the grave of Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, and laid next to the uncle who raised him and was buried there forty-three years before. The two men's own biographies record the adjacency; the cemetery's does not list either of them among its notable dead. The ground is known today as the Sheikh Ma'ruf cemetery, and the coordinates used here are its own, not the ones the guidebooks copy from each other.
suggested_refs: The Shunuziyya, today Sheikh Ma'ruf cemetery, Karkh, Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the disciple on the wood
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Twelve years after Junayd is buried, al-Hallaj is taken out of nine years of prison, mutilated and beheaded in this city, and what is left of him is burned and thrown into the Tigris. Later Sufi hagiography brings Junayd back to sign the death warrant, in the gown of the academy rather than the Sufi robe, and tells the story for centuries to people who can count. The historical Junayd has been dead since 910. The legend needs him at the trial, so the legend fetches him.
suggested_refs: The trial and execution of al-Hallaj, Baghdad, 26 March 922

stops.name: Bestam, a false ascent under his name
stops.date_confidence: attested; 395 AH
stops.campa: In 395 of the Hijra an embellished account of the heavenly ascent circulates under the name of a certain Abu'l-Qasim, and readers take it for the work of Abu'l-Qasim al-Junayd. The text belongs to the Bistami material, from the town under the Alburz where Abu Yazid is buried. The man who put Bayazid's Persian into Arabic ends up credited with a Bistami forgery a century after his death, by way of nothing more than a shared kunya and a careless copyist.
suggested_refs: The 395/1005 mi'raj text falsely circulated under al-Junayd's name

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn Arabi's twelve days
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ibn Arabi passes through on his way east and stays twelve days in the City of Peace, which his own account names as the city of al-Junayd and of al-Hallaj before him. Three centuries have welded the two names into a single address, and the graves on the west bank are a station on the road by now rather than a discovery. The Andalusian will be buried at Salihiyya in Damascus, and will acquire six hundred years later a neighbour out of Algeria who came here first.
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's twelve days in Baghdad, 1205, on the journey east

stops.name: Baghdad, the boy at the tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas entry for Rumi
stops.campa: A family out of Balkh, running west ahead of the Mongols, halts in Baghdad, and Baha al-Din takes his son to pray at the graves of the old masters, Junayd and Ma'ruf al-Karkhi among them. Jalal al-Din is twelve or so. He will write, in Persian, in an Anatolian town he has not yet heard the name of, verse after verse on annihilation in God, in a vocabulary this grave handed to the language three hundred years before he was born. Nobody at the graveside tells him so.
suggested_refs: The flight of Baha al-Din's household from Balkh, through Baghdad, 1219

stops.name: Nishapur, Attar writes him down
stops.date_confidence: the work is dated late twelfth to early thirteenth century, commonly c. 1220, before Attar's death in 1221
stops.campa: Farid al-Din Attar compiles the Tadhkirat al-Awliya across most of a long life at Nishapur, and the chapter on Abu'l-Qasim al-Junayd fixes the shape in which the Persian world, and then the European one, will receive him: the sober master, the boy who defined thankfulness, the teacher who refused Shibli the jewel. Attar is killed when the Mongols take Nishapur in 1221. Most of what is quoted as Junayd's has passed through his hands on the way here.
suggested_refs: Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter 'Abo 'l-Qasem al-Jonaid'

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn Battuta at the bridge of boats
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas entry for Ibn Battuta
stops.campa: Ibn Battuta of Tangier crosses the pontoon bridge into a Baghdad four centuries past Junayd's, and notes what every traveller notes: that al-Hallaj was killed here and his ashes thrown into the river. The tombs on the west bank are on the itinerary now, a fixed item, visited between the markets and the colleges. The city he describes is a provincial one under Mongol governors, half its quarters unrebuilt since the sack, and its principal export by now is the memory of the men who taught in it.
suggested_refs: Ibn Battuta's Rihla on Baghdad and its bridge of boats, 1327

stops.name: Baghdad, the Algerian at the Jilani shrine
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas entry for Abdelkader
stops.campa: A boy from the Wadi al-Hammam, named Abd al-Qadir after the Baghdad saint whose order his father keeps, kneels at the tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani on his first pilgrimage. The Qadiriyya's chain of transmission runs back through this city's sober Sufism, Junayd's own, three centuries before al-Jilani was born in it. The boy will fight France for seventeen years, be imprisoned in a château on the Loire, and stand between a mob and the Christians of Damascus on the authority of a discipline assembled here.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani at Bab al-Sheikh, Baghdad

stops.name: London, the Rasa'il in print
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ali Hassan Abdel-Kader publishes the surviving epistles for the Gibb Memorial Trust, Arabic and English on facing terms with a biographical study, and a body of writing that had circulated in manuscript for a thousand years acquires page numbers. Edinburgh reissues it in paperback for the Trust in 2014. A scan titled The Rasa'il of Junayd goes up on the Internet Archive in 2017 carrying no author, no translator and no date, so whether it is this edition cannot be established from the page.
suggested_refs: Abdel-Kader, The Life, Personality and Writings of al-Junayd, Gibb Memorial Series, Luzac 1962
sources: Internet Archive item 'The Rasail Of Junayd', uploaded 4 November 2017

stops.name: Baghdad, the shrine rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Arabic sources give the renovation as 1980
stops.campa: The grave is enclosed in a mosque and shrine complex of some 2,500 square metres in Karkh, and pilgrims come to it as a station rather than as a curiosity. No state memorial to Junayd exists apart from the religious building, and no museum: the commemoration is a shrine or it is nothing at all. That is a narrower gap than the one usually reported, which claims he has no monument beyond a bare grave, and which this building contradicts simply by standing on the spot.
suggested_refs: The Junayd al-Baghdadi mosque and shrine, Karkh, renovated 1980

stops.name: Baghdad, the highway over the dead
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The government orders exhumations across the Sheikh Ma'ruf cemetery to clear ground for a road meant to ease the traffic of a city of millions. Clergy issue a fatwa permitting the removals; residents refuse and protest; the authorities settle instead on building a bridge over the cemetery, and leave the families who did move their dead to pay for it themselves. The ground where Junayd lies beside his uncle now runs under a flyover. What the shrine looks like after all this is documented nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The 2023 dispute over the Sheikh Ma'ruf cemetery and the Baghdad road scheme
